body:
Why nuclear exports are controlled

Nuclear power programmes may require imported fuel, equipment, materials and technology. Some of these items can also have sensitive applications. Countries exporting nuclear-related items therefore use export controls to reduce the risk of their misuse.

The Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG) is a group of nuclear supplier governments that coordinate guidelines for nuclear and nuclear-related exports. It developed after India's 1974 nuclear test, which demonstrated the proliferation concerns associated with nuclear technology supplied for peaceful purposes. The NSG began its consultations in 1975.

The NSG is not an international treaty and is not the IAEA. Its guidelines are implemented through the export-control laws and decisions of participating governments. According to the NSG's published participant information consulted for this lesson, it has 48 Participating Governments.

What the NSG guidelines cover

  • Part 1: Nuclear material, equipment and technology identified in the nuclear export guidelines and their trigger list.
  • Part 2: Nuclear-related dual-use equipment, materials, software and technology that may have both civilian and sensitive applications.

Exporting governments consider safeguards requirements, assurances about peaceful use and other applicable conditions before permitting controlled transfers. Because the NSG is an export-control arrangement, it does not itself inspect nuclear facilities or grant reactor operating licences.

How India's civil nuclear cooperation changed

For many years, India's position outside the NPT and the absence of comprehensive safeguards across its programme limited access to international nuclear trade. A series of diplomatic and legal decisions created a route for cooperation involving India's declared civilian nuclear facilities.

  1. 2005: India and the United States announced an initiative to expand civil nuclear cooperation. The initiative depended on separation of declared civilian and military nuclear facilities and appropriate safeguards commitments.
  2. 1 August 2008: The IAEA Board of Governors approved the India-specific civilian safeguards agreement.
  3. 6 September 2008: The NSG agreed by consensus to an India-specific exception from its general full-scope-safeguards requirement for qualifying peaceful nuclear transfers.
  4. 10 October 2008: India and the United States signed their bilateral agreement for cooperation concerning peaceful uses of nuclear energy, commonly called the 123 Agreement.
  5. 11 May 2009: India's civilian safeguards agreement with the IAEA entered into force.
  6. 25 July 2014: India's Additional Protocol entered into force.

Why it is called the 123 Agreement

The name 123 Agreement comes from Section 123 of the United States Atomic Energy Act of 1954, which governs agreements for certain forms of American nuclear cooperation with other countries. It is a bilateral cooperation agreement, not an article of the NPT and not an agreement that made India an NSG participant.

What the 2008 NSG exception did not mean

The NSG exception helped make international civil nuclear trade with India possible despite its non-membership of the NPT and the absence of full-scope safeguards. It did not make India a party to the NPT, confer membership of the NSG, remove all export restrictions, or allow unrestricted nuclear transfers.

Actual cooperation remains subject to supplier-country laws, applicable NSG guidelines, bilateral agreements and safeguards conditions. The civilian facilities and materials declared for international cooperation must be distinguished from facilities outside those civilian commitments.

Three separate instruments: The IAEA safeguards agreement governs verification, the NSG exception concerns participating suppliers' export rules, and the 123 Agreement provides the bilateral India-US cooperation framework.

Prelims focus

  • NSG emerged following the 1974 Indian nuclear test and began consultations in 1975.
  • NSG has 48 Participating Governments according to its published participant list consulted in November 2026.
  • NSG is an export-control arrangement, not a treaty.
  • India-specific NSG exception: 6 September 2008.
  • India-US 123 Agreement signed: 10 October 2008.
  • Trap: India's 2008 NSG exception did not make India an NSG participant or an NPT party.

[Sources: Nuclear Suppliers Group, Frequently Asked Questions, sections What is the NSG, Who participates in the NSG and Why was the NSG created; Ministry of External Affairs, India's Foreign Relations 2008, section on the Civil Nuclear Initiative and NSG decision of 6 September 2008; US Department of State, US-India Civil Nuclear Cooperation Initiative, 2008, section Current Status and Background; IAEA Office of Legal Affairs, India Country Factsheet, Safeguards Agreements; consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: India's civil nuclear cooperation developed through separate diplomatic, safeguards and export-control steps.

body:
What the CTBT seeks to prohibit

The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) seeks to prohibit nuclear test explosions and all other nuclear explosions, whether conducted underground, underwater or in the atmosphere. It is intended to constrain the development and improvement of nuclear explosive capabilities and strengthen international non-proliferation and disarmament efforts.

The United Nations General Assembly adopted the CTBT on 10 September 1996, and it opened for signature on 24 September 1996.

The CTBT must not be confused with the NPT. The NPT addresses the proliferation of nuclear weapons and contains provisions on peaceful nuclear uses and disarmament. The CTBT specifically addresses nuclear explosions. It does not prohibit ordinary electricity generation by nuclear reactors.

Why the CTBT has not entered into force

Under Article XIV, the treaty enters into force 180 days after all 44 states listed in Annex 2 have deposited their instruments of ratification, but not earlier than 2 years after it opened for signature. These states were identified because of specified nuclear capabilities and participation in the treaty negotiations at the relevant time.

Status at 15 November 2026: The United Nations Treaty Collection recorded 188 signatories and 179 ratifications, but the CTBT had not entered into force. The required ratifications of 9 Annex 2 states were still outstanding.

Annex 2 statusStates
Not signedIndia, Pakistan, North Korea
Signed but without an effective ratificationChina, Egypt, Iran, Israel, Russia, United States

Russia ratified the CTBT in 2000 but revoked its ratification in 2023. It therefore remains among the Annex 2 states whose ratification is required. Ratification by a large majority of countries does not remove the treaty's specific entry-into-force condition.

How possible nuclear tests are monitored

Although the treaty is not yet in force, the Preparatory Commission for the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO) operates and develops an international verification system. Its monitoring network uses 4 complementary technologies.

  • Seismic monitoring: Detects vibrations travelling through the Earth, including signals that may be associated with underground explosions.
  • Hydroacoustic monitoring: Detects sound waves travelling through the oceans.
  • Infrasound monitoring: Detects very low-frequency sound waves travelling through the atmosphere.
  • Radionuclide monitoring: Detects radioactive particles or gases that may provide evidence of a nuclear event.

Monitoring data must be analysed and interpreted. A seismic signal, for example, may require further assessment to distinguish an explosion from an earthquake or another event. The purpose of combining monitoring methods is to improve the ability to detect and assess suspicious events.

Under the CTBT's planned verification regime, on-site inspections are a treaty mechanism that becomes available after the treaty enters into force. They should not be confused with the international monitoring activities already operating before entry into force.

India's position on nuclear testing

India has not signed the CTBT. Following its nuclear tests at Pokhran in May 1998, India announced a voluntary moratorium on further nuclear test explosions.

A voluntary moratorium is a policy commitment declared by a state. It is not the same as becoming a party to the CTBT and accepting its treaty obligations. The United Nations records no further Indian nuclear test explosions after 1998 in its historical account of nuclear testing.

NPT: Preventing the spread of nuclear weapons. CTBT: Prohibiting nuclear explosions under a treaty that has not yet entered into force. IAEA safeguards: Verifying covered nuclear material and activities. These instruments have related but distinct purposes.

Prelims focus

  • CTBT adopted: 10 September 1996.
  • CTBT opened for signature: 24 September 1996.
  • Entry into force requires ratification by all 44 Annex 2 states.
  • As at 15 November 2026, 9 Annex 2 ratifications were outstanding and the treaty was not in force.
  • Monitoring methods: seismic, hydroacoustic, infrasound and radionuclide.
  • Trap: India's voluntary testing moratorium does not mean that India has signed or ratified the CTBT.

[Sources: United Nations Treaty Collection, Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty, Article XIV and treaty status dated 15 November 2026; CTBTO Preparatory Commission, Frequently Asked Questions, sections Overview, Entry into Force and Verification; United Nations, International Day against Nuclear Tests, History, section Breaking the de facto moratorium; consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Four monitoring technologies detect different physical signals to assess suspected nuclear explosions; treaty inspection powers follow entry into force.
pictures.caption: Four monitoring methods provide different kinds of evidence about possible nuclear explosions.

title: The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty and Its Verification System

body:
Why civil liability matters in nuclear energy

Nuclear safety regulation tries to prevent accidents. Civil nuclear liability addresses a different question: if a nuclear incident causes legally recognised damage, who is responsible for paying compensation, and under what conditions?

Compensation rules matter because a nuclear incident may cause personal injury, property damage and other recognised losses. Victims need an identifiable route for making claims. Governments, plant operators and equipment suppliers also need to know how the law allocates financial responsibility.

The Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010

India enacted the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010 to provide a special framework for compensation for nuclear damage.

The Act generally channelled liability to the operator of the nuclear installation. It adopted a strict, no-fault liability approach for the operator: an eligible claimant did not have to establish ordinary negligence by the operator as the basis of liability under the Act. The statutory framework nevertheless contained defined conditions, exclusions and monetary limits.

Under Section 17, after paying compensation, the operator could exercise a right of recourse in specified circumstances. These included:

  • A right of recourse expressly provided in a written contract.
  • A nuclear incident caused by an act of a supplier or its employee, including defective equipment or materials or substandard services.
  • An act or omission by an individual done with the intent to cause nuclear damage.

Recourse means seeking recovery from another responsible party after paying compensation. It is distinct from the victim's initial claim. The supplier did not automatically become the party directly responsible for paying all victims simply because it supplied equipment.

The SHANTI Act, 2025

Parliament subsequently enacted the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India Act, 2025, commonly called the SHANTI Act. It is Act 39 of 2025, received presidential assent on 20 December 2025 and was published in the Gazette on 21 December 2025.

The SHANTI Act establishes a broader legislative framework for nuclear activities, regulatory oversight, participation by eligible licensed entities and compensation for nuclear damage. Its Section 91 provides for repeal of the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010, with savings for specified existing arrangements when the relevant provisions commence.

The enacted Act continues an operator-centred compensation approach. Under Sections 13 and 14, it specifies liability limits and circumstances in which the Central Government bears responsibility. These include liability exceeding the operator's statutory limit, incidents at Central Government-owned installations, and incidents caused by exceptional grave natural disasters, armed conflict, hostility, civil war, insurrection or terrorism. The Act sets an overall incident-liability amount at the rupee equivalent of 300 million Special Drawing Rights, subject to the statutory provision for a higher amount specified by the Central Government. Its Second Schedule gives different operator-liability limits according to the installation category, ranging from ₹100 crore to ₹3,000 crore.

The new Act also requires operators to obtain insurance or other financial security covering their statutory liability before operation; this requirement excludes installations owned by the Central Government. Its Section 16 contains the operator's right of recourse after compensation, but lists 2 grounds: an express written contractual right, or an individual's act or omission intended to cause nuclear damage. Unlike Section 17(b) of the 2010 Act, it does not separately list supplier defects as an independent statutory ground of recourse. A written contract may still provide for recourse according to the law and its terms.

Issue2010 ActEnacted SHANTI Act, 2025
Initial compensation responsibilityGenerally channelled to the operatorOperator-centred framework, with specified government responsibility
Right of recourseWritten contract, specified supplier acts, or intentional harmWritten contract or intentional harm
Regulatory and sector frameworkSeparate atomic-energy and civil-liability statutesBroader framework covering licensing, safety oversight and liability
ImplementationReference framework before the relevant replacement provisions commenceCommencement depends on government notification

The difference between enactment and commencement

Section 1(2) of the SHANTI Act provides that its provisions come into force on dates appointed by Central Government notification in the Official Gazette. Different provisions may commence on different dates. Therefore, passage of the Act and presidential assent do not, by themselves, establish that every provision has become operative.

The Department of Atomic Energy stated on 23 July 2026 that implementing rules were being drafted and that applications for private-sector licences would be considered after notification of the rules. Draft SHANTI Rules and Regulations were circulated for public comment in August 2026, with comments invited until 4 September 2026. Draft rules are proposals, not automatically enforceable final rules.

Legal-status qualification at the 16 November 2026 content cutoff: The SHANTI Act's enactment is established. Its substantive provisions must be assessed according to commencement notifications, not merely the date of assent. The verified government implementation update of 23 July 2026 and the subsequent August 2026 draft-rule process do not establish that all replacement provisions have commenced.

International liability cooperation

India is also a party to the Convention on Supplementary Compensation for Nuclear Damage (CSC). The IAEA's India country record gives 4 May 2016 as the date it entered into force for India. The CSC concerns arrangements for compensation following nuclear damage. It is not a nuclear-testing treaty or an IAEA safeguards agreement.

Prelims focus

  • The Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act was enacted in 2010.
  • Section 17 of the 2010 Act expressly included certain supplier acts as a recourse ground.
  • SHANTI Act: Act 39 of 2025; presidential assent on 20 December 2025.
  • SHANTI Act Section 16 contains written-contract and intentional-harm recourse grounds.
  • SHANTI Act Section 1(2) makes commencement dependent on government notification.
  • Trap: An enacted replacement law must not be treated as fully operational without checking its commencement provisions.

[Sources: Government of India, Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010, Sections 4, 6 and 17; Department of Atomic Energy, Frequently Asked Questions and Answers on the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, questions 8-12; Gazette of India, SHANTI Act, 2025, Act 39 of 2025, Sections 1, 13-16 and 91 and Second Schedule, published 21 December 2025; Press Information Bureau, Department of Atomic Energy, Parliament Question on Private Sector Participation in Nuclear Energy, 23 July 2026; PRS Legislative Research, August 2026 Monthly Policy Review, section on draft SHANTI Rules and Regulations; IAEA Office of Legal Affairs, India Country Factsheet, Convention on Supplementary Compensation; consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Operator compensation comes first; later recourse differs because the enacted 2025 law omits a separate express supplier-defect ground.
pictures.caption: Operator liability and subsequent recourse are different stages of compensation.

title: Civil Nuclear Liability and India's Changing Legal Framework
